title: The Long Lantern
premise: In 1912 Cardiff, Emrys Villalobos drives for suffragist organizer Bronwen Hale, and quietly reads every letter she carries — until a census taker's probing questions expose that Emrys has been intercepting correspondence that could name the workshop's secret printing circle. With the workshop under surveillance and a raid imminent, Emrys must choose between protecting Bronwen, whom she has come to love, and telling the truth that could save an innocent printer from prison. In the end, Emrys testifies to protect the innocent man, the workshop burns in a final act of defiance rather than surrender, and she and Bronwen leave Cardiff together — poorer, hunted, but no longer hiding.
about_author: Astrid Whitlock is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing Welsh suffrage correspondence before turning to fiction. She writes from a cottage on the Gower Peninsula, where she still repairs typewriters by hand.

chapters.title: The Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. A routine census visit to the Hale household turns dangerous when the taker notices Emrys's fluent reading of an addressed envelope. Emrys deflects, but the taker's parting glance lingers. Emotional beat: the quiet dread of a hidden life touched by light for the first time.

chapters.title: Letters Before Delivery
chapters.summary: Flashback-woven chapter in Emrys's POV establishing her habit of reading Bronwen's mail — and how she fell for Bronwen through her words before her face. Emotional beat: tenderness tangled with guilt, the intimacy of stolen reading.

chapters.title: The Workshop Below the Chapel
chapters.summary: Bronwen's POV. She brings Emrys into the secret printing circle beneath a disused chapel, needing a driver who won't talk. Emrys sees the faces of the women and one young printer, Tom Bevan. Emotional beat: belonging offered at a price.

chapters.title: A Census Taker's Memory
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. The census taker, Mr. Pritchard, reappears — not as an official but as a man asking about 'seditious literature.' Emrys realizes he's a Home Office informant. Emotional beat: the hunter's patience; fear sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Letter She Shouldn't Have Read
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. A letter reveals that Tom Bevan is being framed as the circle's leader to protect the women of standing. Emrys holds the proof that could save him — and destroy Bronwen's network. Emotional beat: loyalty and truth pulling in opposite directions.

chapters.title: What Bronwen Asks of Me
chapters.summary: Bronwen's POV. Bronwen asks Emrys to burn the letter, arguing one printer's ruin buys the movement's survival. Emrys refuses — and their first quarble becomes their first confession of feeling. Emotional beat: love declared in the language of disagreement.

chapters.title: Surveillance at the Lamplighters' Arms
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Pritchard corners Emrys at a pub, offering immunity in exchange for names. She stalls, learns the raid is set for Saturday. Emotional beat: the terrible clarity of a deadline; betrayal offered as salvation.

chapters.title: Saturday Comes Early
chapters.summary: Bronwen's POV. The raid arrives two days ahead of schedule — someone inside talked, and Emrys suspects her own stalling was traced. Tom is arrested; the presses are seized. Emotional beat: guilt as a physical wound; the circle fracturing.

chapters.title: The Long Lantern
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV, climax. Emrys testifies at Tom's hearing, reading the intercepted letter aloud to prove his innocence, sacrificing her anonymity and Bronwen's protection. That night, the women burn the chapel workshop themselves rather than let it be evidence. Emotional beat: truth spoken at last, at the cost of everything built in silence.

chapters.title: The Road Out of Cardiff
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs, resolution. Tom walks free; the movement scatters and survives. Bronwen and Emrys meet at the coach yard with two tickets and no plan, choosing each other over duty's ashes. Emotional beat: hard-won belonging — a small light carried forward, not extinguished.
